## Introduction

This traces one institutional function — the stewardship of research data at UCLA — across six
decades and five different institutional homes. It is not a straight line. The unit's name,
organizational home, and formal scope changed repeatedly; what stayed constant was a
responsibility to make research evidence findable, usable, and preserved, extended again and
again to new kinds of evidence as the objects of research changed. A 1961 archive of punch-card
survey data and a 2024 platform processing petabytes of restricted voter records are
recognizably continuous work — the same responsibility carried to new kinds of evidence — but
the scale, the methods, and the institutional stakes changed enormously along the way, and this
account tries not to read today's vocabulary backward onto earlier decades.

A full evidentiary companion — complete people roster, project inventories, visualization
methodology, and open discrepancies not yet resolved — is at
[history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html); this document is the narrative, not the full record.

## The history in 30 seconds

- UCLA's data archive traces to **1961**, when political scientist Dwaine Marvick founded the
  **Political Behavior Archive**.
- It moved through several institutional homes over six decades — never a single continuous
  organization, but a continuous *function*, re-housed as the campus around it changed: a survey
  center (1964), a research institute (1974), a formally-named archive within that institute
  (1977), and finally its own unit inside the UCLA Library (2014).
- Two long-running recurring survey series — **LAMAS** (1970-1976) and its successor **LACSS**
  (1992-2002+) — are the closest thing to a continuous data product across that span, with
  **SCSS** bridging the gap between them.
- One person, **Elizabeth "Libbie" Stephenson**, is documented staffing or directing the archive
  continuously from **1986 to 2016+** — the clearest human through-line across the institutional
  changes.
- In **2018**, the archive's umbrella became the **Data Science Center**, which extended the same
  stewardship mission to new kinds of research data — 3D and spatial capture, restricted/sensitive
  datasets, and curriculum itself as a citable output.

## A note on the author's position

Tim Dennis directed the Social Science Data Archive and the Data Science Center from April 2017
through 2026. For that period this is participant history — written by someone who was in the
events and is also their historian. Three things follow, and are applied throughout:

- Contemporary claims are tied to cited institutional records, not to memory or recollection.
  Because the author took part in these events, the recent decades are held to a higher
  documentation standard than the earlier ones, not a looser one.
- Evaluative judgments — what worked, what mattered, what was lost — are marked as judgments, not
  stated as fact.
- Work done by a team is credited to the team. Individual attribution is used only where
  authorship, formal authority, or accountability is historically material.

The evidence cutoff for this draft is **2026-08-31**. Before it is finalized the document will be
read by at least one person outside the unit, for factual support, proportion, and treatment of
contrary evidence; that reviewer will be named here. Corrections and version history live in the
project repository. Fuller detail on sources and their limits is in
[Methods and limitations](#methods-and-limitations).

## 1961-1964: The Political Behavior Archive

Political scientist Dwaine Marvick, who had joined UCLA's faculty in 1954, founded the
**Political Behavior Archive (PBA)** in 1961 [@marvickInMemoriam]. The following year, through
Marvick's efforts, UCLA became one of ICPSR's eight founding members [@marvickInMemoriam] —
placing UCLA in the founding cohort of social science data archives internationally, alongside
the Roper Center (1957), Berkeley (1958), and, in the years just after, the UK Data Archive
(1967) and Odum (1969) [@riceSouthall2016]. The PBA's stewardship object was straightforward for
its moment: distributing survey and behavioral data from ICPR, the Roper Public Opinion Research
Center, and local holdings to UCLA researchers [@stilesStephenson2008].

<!-- internal working notes: evidence/marvick-biography-and-papers.md; evidence/stiles-stephenson-2008-ifla.md; evidence/icpsr-history.md; evidence/rice-southall-2016-ch1.md -->

## 1964-1974: The Survey Research Center years

The Survey Research Center (SRC) formed at UCLA in 1964, and the PBA merged into it
[@stilesStephenson2008]. Marvick's own unpublished proposal that August — *"Plans for the
Development of a Social Science Archival Data Library in the UCLA Survey Research Center"*
[@marvick1967proposal] — set out the archival concept that would eventually become SSDA, though
the document itself hasn't been located yet (see [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html)). The SRC's stewardship
object during this decade was the **Los Angeles Metropolitan Area Surveys (LAMAS)**: ten waves,
1970-1976, a shared omnibus survey repeated roughly twice yearly with rotating
researcher-submitted questions [@stilesStephenson2008; @pawlockiStephenson1988].

The decade's clearest external consequence came from outside the archive itself: around 1970,
UCLA Library's Public Affairs Service, under Mary Ryan, purchased 1970 census tapes from
DUALabs — the library's first foray into numeric data, and one cited nationally as an
early/paradigm case for library involvement in machine-readable data [@roweRyan1974; @dodd1982].

<!-- internal working notes: evidence/stiles-stephenson-2008-ifla.md; evidence/lamas-scss-lacss-series.md; evidence/dodd-1982-library-trends-mrdf.md -->

## 1974-1977: ISSR, and the archive gets a name

The **Institute for Social Science Research (ISSR)** was established in 1974, incorporating the
SRC and its archival data library, under founding director Howard Freeman
[@stilesStephenson2008]. Three years later, then-Associate Director **Donald Treiman** formalized
that archival data library into a newly-named service unit — the **Social Science Data Archive
(SSDA)**, housed within ISSR — and ISSR posted its first Data Archivist job opening
[@stilesStephenson2008; @pawlockiStephenson1988]. (1974 and 1977 are genuinely separate events,
not one founding date told two ways — see the timeline above.)

The consequence worth noting here runs against the direction most of this history moves in:
around 1980, when UCLA Library declined to purchase 1980 census tapes, ISSR/SSDA took them on
instead, along with all associated support and storage — numeric-data stewardship moved from the
Library to the Archive [@stilesStephenson2008], the reverse of the direction it would move in
2014.

<!-- internal working notes: evidence/stiles-stephenson-2008-ifla.md (most precise account); dsc-evidence-registry/claims/issr-transfer-1977.yaml (4 independent corroborations) -->

## 1977-2014: SSDA under ISSR

SSDA's recurring survey work continued under the LAMAS model, renamed and reshaped: the
**Southern California Social Survey (SCSS)**, then the **Los Angeles County Social Survey
(LACSS)**, confirmed running through 1992-2002 (see [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html) for the full series
detail). By the 1990s the archive had become, in its own staff's words, "the de facto
campus-wide data service unit," serving public health, education, policy studies, law, and
management, not just social science departments [@stilesStephenson2008].

The clearest human through-line for this entire era is **Elizabeth "Libbie" Stephenson**,
documented as archive staff and later Director continuously from 1986 to 2016 or later
[@pawlockiStephenson1988; @stephenson2013dodd; @dotyEtal2014] — see People and stewardship below.
Read in hindsight, her career-long work on bibliographic control (with Sue Dodd's scholarship,
IASSIST, and ICPSR) is early data-citation practice, in the vocabulary a much later era would use
for the same underlying task: making data properly identified and findable. The era's clearest
external consequence was cross-national: the Intergenerational Stratification and Mobility File
(ISMF), built with Harry Ganzeboom (Free University, Amsterdam) and Donald Treiman, funded by the
Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research [@stilesStephenson2008].

## 2014-2018: The Library MOU, and a change of director

The 2014 (effective)/2015 (executed) MOU transferred SSDA from the Social Sciences Division to
the UCLA Library — the first time the archive exited ISSR to become a standalone unit. It
carried 2.0 FTE, ~$245K in permanent funds, and ~$29K in subscriptions (ICPSR, Roper, UC
Berkeley/SDA, Colectica/Algenta); staff continuity included Elizabeth Stephenson and Jina
"Jamie" Jamison [@uclaSsdaMou2014].

**In April 2017, Tim Dennis was hired as Director of SSDA, succeeding Stephenson**, who had led
the archive since at least 1986.[^tim-hire] This is the point this history's own author enters
the institutional record — see Methods and limitations for how that's handled. That November,
Dennis presented "Library Data Archive" to UCLA Library staff, already framing 1961-2017 as one
continuous arc under the tagline "Providing archive and data services since 1961"
[@dennis2017deck]. In 2018, the **Data Science Center (DSC)** formed as the umbrella program —
the point the archive's function formally broadened beyond social science.

[^tim-hire]: Tim Dennis, personal account, 2026-08-09.

<!-- internal working notes: evidence/ssda-library-mou.md; evidence/ucla-ssda-lineage-2017-deck.md -->

## 2018-present: The Data Science Center

### Continuity, not rupture

The 2018 rebrand changed the unit's name and broadened its scope; it didn't replace what came
before. `ucla-data-archive_old`, a repository built around the "Data Archive" identity — its
collections policies, terms, deposit and preservation practices — was created July 2017 and
actively maintained through May 2020, two years past the point the org's formal name became
"Data Science Center." The archive's core function (UCLA Dataverse hosting, the direct
descendant of the LAMAS/SCSS/LACSS lineage) continued operating underneath the new name the
whole time, and later broadened its own scope directly: DSC now hosts Dataverse collections for
external UCLA research units spanning law (UCLA Law Behind Bars Data Project, 1,169 items),
LGBT policy research reaching ICPSR nationally (the Williams Institute's TransPop and
Generations studies), and archaeology at a scale (Cotsen Institute/DIG, 6,360 items) larger than
the archive's entire historical corpus combined. Full detail: [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html).

### What stayed constant, and what changed

Across five institutional homes and 60-plus years, the constant has been a responsibility to
make research evidence findable, usable, and preserved — extended, era by era, to whatever kind
of evidence researchers were producing. What changed after 2018 is the *range* of objects that
responsibility covers: not just survey datasets, but 3D and spatial capture, restricted and
sensitive data requiring governed computational access, and curriculum itself treated as a
citable research output. Read in sequence, that range traces something like data citation → open
and FAIR data → open science → software curation → computationally-intensive research support —
but that sequence is a retrospective way of describing what changed, not a plan any era was
executing. Three concrete cases carry this era's evidence.

#### DataSquad: extending stewardship into direct research support

Tim founded UCLA DataSquad, an undergraduate student consulting program, in 2021, seeded in part
by Norman Powell's philanthropic gift (see People and stewardship). In the 2023-2025 review
period alone, DSC and DataSquad together documented 1,175 service interactions, of which 190
were direct student consultations — capacity that let senior staff take on more complex
requests while giving students substantive research-support experience. DataSquad students
worked on the two projects below; graduating students have gone on to McKinsey & Company,
Amazon, AIG, and Stanford.[^dataSquad-source]

[^dataSquad-source]: Tim Dennis, Statement of Professional Achievements, 2023-2025 review
period, self-reported (see [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html) on evidentiary treatment of review-document
claims).

#### Redivis: from data possession to governed access

Before January 2023, UCLA had no compliant environment for restricted, multi-terabyte national
datasets — no secure way to give a student voter-file access, no environment for merging
FERPA/PII/PHI/HIPAA-restricted data. Tim selected and licensed Redivis, negotiated access to
restricted national datasets, navigated P3/P4 compliance approval, and launched the platform in
January 2023, designing its governance (a 50-seat model with data-use-agreement controls) so
that routine access requests wouldn't bottleneck on him.

Adoption was real and fast: the platform grew from 5 workflows and 444 GB processed in its first
year to 2.9 petabytes in 2024. Working with a UCLA Political Science research group (Straus,
Thompson, Ferrer, and Geyn), DSC provided both the platform and the data, and that group
published in *American Political Science Review*, *PNAS*, *British Journal of Political
Science*, and *AEJ: Applied Economics*.[^redivis-source] A related dataset carries its own DOI
(UCLA Library, *L2 Voter History and Demographic Dataset*, 2023, doi:10.60603/D33W2T), and the
work was presented at FORCE11 2024, where doctoral researcher Graham Straus put the
institutional-continuity point directly: "What happens when I leave UCLA? Will people know how
the dataset was constructed? Yes!"

The infrastructure enabled this work; it didn't produce the scholarship itself — DSC's
documented role is selecting, implementing, and supporting the platform and data access, not
authorship. Read against the throughline above, Redivis's significance isn't primarily an
"ML/AI" story — it's the point stewardship came to include *governed computation*, not just
acquiring and describing open files.

[^redivis-source]: Tim Dennis, Statement of Professional Achievements and Data Summary,
2023-2025 review period, self-reported; the publication venues and Straus quote are the
independently-checkable part of this claim.

#### The IMLS grant: curriculum as a citable research output

As Project Director on a federal IMLS grant (RE-252335-OLS-22, $237,839, awarded FY2022,
"Lessons for Librarians in Open Science Principles and Methods") [@imls-re252335], Tim delivered
15 peer-reviewed open-science lessons against a proposed 14, treating curriculum as a first-class
research output rather than just teaching material: DOI assignment through Zenodo, CRediT
taxonomy for author contributions, ORCID integration, and Citation File Format metadata. Twenty-
eight co-authors across 14 institutions took part; three lessons, including Data Management
Plans 101, achieved formal adoption into the worldwide Library Carpentry curriculum through
Tim's chairship of its Curriculum Advisory Committee.

This is the era's clearest instance of the "software curation" and "open science" stages of the
throughline above — and the one with the strongest independent evidence, since a federal grant
award is verifiable independent of anyone's own account of it.

### People and funding

Norman Powell's philanthropic gifts (a data scientist position, a deep learning machine and DSC
space in the Charles E. Young Research Library, and DataSquad's seed funding — separately from
his precisely-dated $5 million December 2016 gift endowing the University Librarian position)
made much of this era's expansion possible. Doug Daniels, Emerging Technologies Librarian since
2013 and UCLA's **Librarian of the Year 2026**, built the "Lux Lab" and its 3D/spatial data
capability into exactly this kind of extended stewardship — including a direct link to Powell's
patronage (Doug LiDAR-scanned Powell Library itself, and gave recurring demos to the Powell
Society donor circle, 2017-2019). Leigh Phan's role evolved from programmer to data scientist
over this period. Full detail on all of this era's people: [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html).

## Research impact

Two different things get measured here, and they answer different questions.

### Historical traces of reuse

**Holdings activity** shows when the archive's deposited datasets were originally collected, by
decade — a proxy for how active the archive itself was. **Citation evidence** shows which of
that data is documented as having been used in later published research — a proxy for downstream
value, not for the archive's own activity. They don't share an axis, and shouldn't be read
against each other directly: a decade with heavy collecting activity doesn't necessarily produce
more citations, and citations can (and here, do) arrive decades after collection.

### Contemporary research enabled

The 2018-present section above develops three cases in full — DataSquad, Redivis, and the IMLS
grant — with their evidence and its limits. Summarized:

| Case | What's independently checkable |
|---|---|
| Redivis / L2 restricted data | Publication venues (APSR, PNAS, BJPolS, AEJ), a public dataset DOI, a public FORCE11 presentation |
| IMLS open-science grant | A federal grant award record, public lesson repositories, Library Carpentry's own adoption record |
| DataSquad | Student placement outcomes (self-reported); the two projects it contributed to (Carceral Ecologies, BioCritical Studies Lab) drew independent national media coverage |

## Methods and limitations

The author's position is stated up front, in "A note on the author's position." Tim Dennis
directed the unit for the recent decades this history covers, and is separately the author of
documents (a grant proposal, reorg-response material) that draw on some of the same facts for
advocacy. A repository boundary doesn't change that. What this project does instead:

- The author's role, and this project's relationship to `ospo_datasquad_grant`, are stated
  plainly rather than left for the reader to discover.
- Facts are sourced to a claim register (`dsc-evidence-registry`), not asserted from memory —
  see `claims/ssda-*`, `claims/icpsr-*`, `claims/issr-*`, `claims/dennis-*`, `claims/dsc-*` there
  for what's verified vs. disputed vs. self-reported.
- Documented facts are kept separate from institutional interpretation; discontinuities, gaps,
  and contested points are stated as such, not smoothed over — see README.md "Known gaps" and
  [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html) "Open discrepancies."
- `ospo_datasquad_grant` may cite this project's evidence, but it is not independent
  corroboration of a claim that traces back to the same author.
- **Self-reported achievement claims** (much of the 2018-present detail comes from Tim's and
  Doug's own internal personnel-review documents) are treated as discovery sources, not sole
  public evidence. Where independent corroboration exists (press coverage, award records,
  publication venues, grant award pages), the claim is included and the corroboration is what's
  cited. Where only the review document supports a claim, it's either omitted or explicitly
  attributed as a self-reported account — see [history-companion.qmd](history-companion.html)
  for what's been held to that standard.
- The evidence cutoff is 2026-08-31. Before the draft is finalized it is reviewed by at least
  one person outside the unit with relevant historical/archival expertise, for factual support,
  proportion, and treatment of contrary evidence; that reviewer is named in "A note on the
  author's position."
